REPLAY, admission-review create and delete only. Both routes decided `this is a fresh command` from something that is not admitted truth: create re-read live governance posture (which stamps its own wall clock) into the payload, so every retry was byte-different under one key and took 409 event_stream_same_key_different_bytes; delete answered 404 from an absent projection before admission was ever reached, so the substrate's replay scan never ran on the very record the first attempt had removed. Both now consult the durable admitted history for the caller's key first, through one shared pure read — mutation_event_foundation::prior_admission_for_key — built on the existing read_owner_scoped_history and the immutable request scope. The probe binds no scope and admits no operation, and answers None rather than a status for a foreign principal so it cannot become an existence oracle.

The posture snapshot is still WRITTEN and still admitted as evidence of gate state at review time; it is excluded from replay IDENTITY only, on both sides of the comparison, so a genuinely changed command under an admitted key still refuses with the substrate's own 409 and event_stream_same_key_different_bytes. A create replay answers with the CURRENT projection when one exists, and on that path writes NOTHING — not the review and not its candidate. When the projection is absent it is repaired from the LATEST admitted nonterminal entry, not from the create: rebuilding from the create restored the create-time decision, findings and reviewer AND re-projected the create's head over a stream that had moved, so every later patch and the delete presented that stale head and were refused event_stream_expected_head_conflict permanently — a repair that wedged the record it repaired. created_at still comes from the original create, updated_at and admitted_head from the latest entry, and a history whose last entry this plane cannot project refuses 500 marketplace_review_history_unclassified rather than falling back to create bytes. Repair may RESTORE an absent candidate backlink, fail-closed; it never takes one that already names a different, newer review, and never touches the candidate's updated_at in that case. A candidate may carry several reviews and admission_review_ref is last-writer-wins, so only a FRESH create is entitled to write it.

TERMINAL-TRUTH FENCE, required before this cut could be integrated. Reading the admitted history early is what makes create replay possible, and it is also what made repair-over-a-deleted-review REACHABLE: the previous moved-posture 409 refused the retry before the substrate's own replay was ever consulted, so no code path could resurrect the record. It is therefore a behaviour this cut would have introduced, not an inherited one, and it is fenced rather than recorded. A create replay now refuses 409 marketplace_review_removed — carrying the terminal admitted_head, and carrying no record — when a marketplace.review.delete is admitted after the create it would replay. It writes nothing on that path: no projection, no candidate backlink, no event. This is the same rule the delete path applies from the other side, so both directions agree that an admitted terminal transition decides existence and no earlier fact may be replayed over it. Reviewing the candidate again requires a new idempotency_key, which mints its own resource on its own stream.

The review's CANDIDATE deletion is weighed too, and earlier: command validation is unchanged and still resolves candidate_ref before the history is read, so a retry whose candidate no longer resolves refuses 400 marketplace_ref_unresolved and can never write a backlink onto a record that is gone — including on the repair branch, where the review projection is also absent.

open_gaps.gap: This plane already has authenticated resource scopes plus direct Agentgres CAS/idempotency for its main state records, but it does not use the shared boundary. Restore cancellation removes staging before the cancelled transition is admitted; restore apply mutates workspace/rollback bytes before the completed transition. progress: LEG 1 (behavior-preserving re-home) LANDED. All twelve event-stream writes on this plane now cross the shared owner-scoped boundary through a local `admit()` adapter over `mutation_event_foundation::admit_owner_scoped_mutation`, replacing the plane's own `append` wrapper. Each write carries the immutable request scope the handler already bound or authorized: the four sites that previously discarded the authorized scope (instance create replay, transition, policy revise, restore action) now capture and pass it, and the backup capture event crosses under the already-authorized storage-profile scope. A local `mutation_refusal()` maps the boundary's refusals back to this plane's existing wire contract (Admission -> `admission_error`, 503 default preserved; Scope -> `scope_refusal`), so no refusal a caller already handles is silently re-statused. `append`/`admit_event_stream_operation` is gone from this module; the source audit now reports shared_foundation_admissions=1, direct_event_admissions=0.

The two effect-ordering defects named in the gap text are FIXED. Restore cancel admitted the cancellation only AFTER deleting the staged bytes: if that append then failed, the plan still read 'prepared' over bytes that were gone, and no reader could tell it was unsatisfiable. Cancel now admits a `restore_plan_cancelling` intent first, so a failure between intent and effect is resumable.

Restore apply deleted the rollback directory — the only copy of the pre-restore workspace — BEFORE admitting completion. A failure in that window left the plan 'applying', the workspace already restored, and nothing left to undo it with: the one state from which neither finishing nor rolling back is possible. Completion is now admitted while the rollback material still exists, and a failure to remove it afterwards is reported as a retained-material cleanup obligation rather than a 500 over a restore that did complete.

`restore_effects_are_admitted_before_they_are_performed` pins both orderings. It asserts source order rather than driving a real restore, because forcing a rename or remove_dir_all to fail mid-transition needs a fixture corpus. It was mutation-checked: reversing the apply ordering makes it fail with the intended message.

The backup projection write after canonical Agentgres admission now says the admission stands and the divergence is replayable, instead of reporting a bare persist failure that reads as though the backup never happened.

LEG 2/3 (restore state machine) LANDED. Restore prepare is now a two-event transition: a `restore_plan_preparing` genesis admitted BEFORE the staging untar (carrying plan identity and source state root), then a `restore_plan_prepared` successor admitted only after the bytes are staged. The orphan-staging dead-end is gone — staged bytes with no admitted plan can no longer occur — and the old `staging.exists()` 409 was removed because a re-presented key now resumes the preparing intent instead of colliding with its own staging.

Restore action replaced the flat `status == 'prepared'` gate with a resume state machine keyed on (admitted status, caller key, on-disk observation): prepared+matching-head runs the initial transition; `cancelling`/`applying` under the SAME caller key resume (re-attempt the missing effect, then admit the terminal transition); a terminal `cancelled`/`completed` under the same key replays the terminal response and admits nothing; anything else is the existing 409 `managed_restore_plan_not_prepared`. The apply renames are convergent — each guarded by its filesystem observation — so a resume performs only the steps a prior interrupted attempt did not.

TERMINAL-TRUTH FENCE landed in the same cut as the replay probe that makes terminal replay reachable: a prepare key re-presented after its plan is cancelled or completed refuses 409 `managed_restore_plan_terminal`, stages nothing, and admits nothing — no create is replayed over an admitted terminal.

Rollback retention is now durable. Completion is admitted WHILE the rollback material still exists; the completed event records `rollback_material_path` and a retention obligation, and when the material cannot be released a `restore_plan_rollback_retained` successor records the obligation in admitted truth — replacing the response-only `cleanup_obligation` JSON that a restart forgot.

An effect-fault seam ships WITH the state machine: a thread-local `RestoreEffectPoint` cell modeled byte-for-byte on `agentgres::event_stream::force_durability_failure_for_this_thread` interrupts prepare/cancel/apply between an admitted transition and the effect it promises, and is a compiled-out no-op in release builds. Both restore handlers were split into sync production halves (`prepare_restore_plan`, `act_on_restore_plan`), and `handle_environment_backup_create` into `capture_environment_backup`, so the tests drive the exact code the routes call.

A shared restore fixture (`build_restore_fixture`) stands up a real Agentgres substrate with a local_private storage profile, a managed instance whose compute_session names the target environment, an on-disk environment record with a materialized workspace, and a completed backup satisfying the hypervisor-environment-backup/v1 contract and `verify_required_exact` — the first end-to-end backup/restore corpus in this repo. The battery drives it: prepare exact-retry across restart; prepare interrupted before/after the untar; cancel interrupted after intent; cancel exact-retry after completion (zero new events); apply interrupted before renames and between the two renames; a completed-append durability fault that leaves the rollback on disk then converges; the terminal-truth fence after both completion and cancellation; a completed-transition exact-retry across restart; and a backup exact-retry admitting exactly one capture and one material. Durability-fault tests are mutex-serialized. The source-order stopgap `restore_effects_are_admitted_before_they_are_performed` was retired — the behavioral tests prove the same orderings by driving real interrupted restores.

open_gaps.correction: The gap text's first acceptance item — 'remove caller-side idempotency scans' — was written as though those scans were unsound. They were read and they are NOT. Both compare COMPLETE request identity: the recipe scan's content_hash is a JCS digest of the entire request minus expected_head and idempotency_key, and ProgramActionRequest has exactly three fields, of which action_identity carries the only two that are semantic. Neither can accept a same-key request with different bytes as a replay. They remain worth removing because each reads the WHOLE stream history per call — O(history) per program step, so O(n^2) across a long training run — and because a second definition of request identity beside the substrate's is exactly what the shared boundary exists to eliminate. That is a duplication and scaling argument, not a correctness one, and this gap should not be cited as evidence of a live idempotency defect.

RESOLVED 2026-08-08 by mechanizing the discriminator in scripts/audit-daemon-mutation-handlers.mjs and wiring npm run check:mutation-handlers, so this list can no longer drift silently. Three distinct causes were found once it was mechanized, and all three had been invisible to hand maintenance:

Rust char literals containing a double-quote (`.trim_matches('"')`) were parsed as string openers, blanking large regions of real code and hiding whole handler signatures. This one is worth recording because the checker's first version reported false negatives against handlers it had already been shown — a checker that answers wrongly is worse than no checker, and it was caught only by testing it against known cases rather than trusting its output.

The handler minted a plaintext trigger token, DISCARDED the persist result, and returned ok:true with the plaintext. The plaintext is shown EXACTLY ONCE and never stored, so over a failed write the operator received a secret that authenticates nowhere while the superseded token stayed fully valid — handle_automation_webhook authorises inbound triggers by comparing sha256(presented) against the durable webhook_token_hash, so the durable hash, not the response, decides what opens the trigger.
